column4: The protected worship sites include prayer houses and mosques “in which God's name is remembered much”; the ayah joins sacred place, the salat word-family, and repeated naming of God.
Abraham's supplication asks God to make him and his descendants establish prayer, then asks that his dua be accepted; salat and supplication meet inside one prayer.
The Messenger recites God's signs and purifies his hearers; within the same surah, 62:9-10 turns that recited instruction into Friday prayer, remembrance, and success.
Those who hold firmly to the Book and establish prayer are joined in one description, making scriptural adherence and salat one enacted practice.
The Arabic Qur'an varies its warnings so that hearers may become reverent or it may produce remembrance in them, directly joining recitation, fear, and new dhikr.
“Stand at night” supplies the bodily posture for the measured Qur'an recitation commanded in 73:4 and the remembrance and prayer later named in 73:8 and 73:20.
The command to recite the Qur'an in a measured manner makes voiced reading the work performed during the night standing of 73:2 and completed by remembrance in 73:8.
These believers remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, then voice a supplication; dhikr, bodily positions, reflection, and dua form one continuous worship scene.
God sees the Prophet “when you rise”; 26:219 specifies his movement among those prostrating, together presenting worship as bodily motion under divine sight.
The Prophet's movement among the prostrators completes 26:218's rising posture and closely matches the section's definition of prayer as a sequence of movements.
People recite the Book yet forget themselves while ordering others to righteousness; 2:45 turns immediately to prayer, exposing the failure to convert recitation into embodied practice.
Seeking help through patience and prayer follows the rebuke of reciters who forget themselves in 2:44; prayer is the difficult enacted answer except for the humble.
The God-conscious establish prayer as an identifying act; 2:5 names this community as the successful, reproducing the section's prayer-to-success relation.
“These are the successful” supplies the outcome of the prayer and faithful response described in 2:3-4.
Those who establish prayer, give zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter enact the same prayer-purification cluster; 31:5 names their success.
The worshippers described in 31:4 are explicitly the successful, again joining established prayer and purification-giving to falah.
The successful believers carefully guard their prayers, giving a positive boundary for the section's warning about people heedless of their prayer.
Preventing God's name from being remembered in His mosques and seeking their ruin reverses the section's scene of the divine name voiced in places of prostration.
Later generations neglect prayer and follow desires; the verse presents loss of salat as the breakdown of the integrated practice.
The people of the Fire confess that they were not among those who prayed, placing omitted prayer on the path to the punishment that the section contrasts with remembrance.
The condemned person neither affirmed nor prayed; 75:32 pairs that failed salat with denial and turning away.
Denial and turning away explain the absence of prayer in 75:31, making salat the bodily counterpart of affirming the message.
“They show off” continues 107:4-5 by identifying the intention behind heedless prayer, distinguishing performed movements from sincere remembrance.
This ayah introduces the person who forbids; 96:10 supplies the forbidden object, a servant at prayer, so the row contributes the hostile act around that worship scene.
They will be called to prostrate but will be unable; 68:43 explains that they had been called to prostration while sound, making the lost bodily response a judgment.
When believers make the public call to prayer, others turn it into mockery and play; the audible summons to salat receives the opposite of a worshipful response.
A suffering person calls on God lying, sitting, or standing, then passes on as though never having called; the same bodily positions that can sustain dhikr here frame forgotten supplication.
A person calls his Lord in distress, then forgets what he had called for after receiving favor; it reverses prayerful remembrance preserved beyond the moment of need.
Those who maintain God's mosques are marked by established prayer, zakat, faith, and reverence, joining worship place, salat, and purification-giving.
The command to set one's face at every place of prostration and call upon God sincerely joins bodily orientation, worship space, and prayer as dua.
Worshippers form the exception to the anxious, withholding human type described around them; 70:23 defines their distinguishing constancy in prayer.
These worshippers are constant in their prayer, supplying a sustained positive counterpart to prayer marked by heedlessness.
A second description says they guard their prayers, repeating the vigilance that distinguishes integrated worship from nominal salat.
The command forbids prostrating to the sun or moon and directs prostration to their Creator, drawing a boundary around the addressee of bodily worship.
Those with the Lord glorify Him night and day without weariness; their unbroken tasbih is a counter-image to forgetful or heedless worship.
The heavenly servants glorify night and day without slackening, another direct formulation of worship untouched by interruption or heedlessness.
Believers are commanded to glorify God morning and evening, giving commanded tasbih the same repeated daily rhythm as prayer.
Jonah's having been among those who glorify is named as the condition of his rescue, complementing the actual tasbih within his supplication in 21:87.
People call on God humbly and secretly in the darkness of land and sea, supplying another quiet-voice scene for prayer understood as dua.
Everything glorifies God's praise although humans do not understand its tasbih; the ayah expands glorification beyond audible words while preserving it as a real act.
Moses asks that the knot in his tongue be untied; 20:28 states the speech purpose, and 20:33-34 later names abundant tasbih and dhikr as the mission this speech serves.
“That they may understand my speech” gives the purpose of the freed tongue in 20:27 before Moses names glorification and remembrance in 20:33-34.
The Prophet is told not to hurry the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to him, setting disciplined reception around the recitation God promises to secure.
The oath by “the Qur'an possessed of remembrance” makes the recited scripture itself the bearer of dhikr.
The prophetic message is described as a reminder to all peoples, supporting the section's inclusion of revealed recitation within dhikr.
The message for which the Prophet asks no payment is “only a reminder to all peoples,” another direct identification of revelation with dhikr.
The Qur'anic proclamation is again described as a reminder to all peoples, preserving the identity between recited message and dhikr.
The revelation is “only a reminder to all peoples,” a repeated formulation that makes Qur'an reception an act of remembrance.
The revelation is called a reminder; 74:55 then turns that objective reminder into the hearer's voluntary remembering.
“Whoever wills may remember it” states the human act elicited by the reminder named in 74:54.
The admonition is called a reminder; 80:12 immediately describes the person who chooses to remember it.
“Whoever wills may remember it” converts the revealed reminder of 80:11 into personal dhikr.
